subject: Culture
title: Sati and Self-Immolation
description: A short lesson to help you apply Sati and Self-Immolation.

hook.text: In 1829, the British banned sati—the practice of a widow burning on her husband's funeral pyre—in India.

buildup.text: Sati was glorified in some Hindu texts as the ultimate act of wifely devotion. Stones marked sati sites as sacred.

discovery.text: Ram Mohan Roy, an Indian reformer, led the campaign against sati before the British ban. Indians fought it first.

twist.text: Many sati cases involved coercion. Families pushed widows onto pyres to claim inheritance.

climax.text: As recently as 1987, a sati case occurred in Rajasthan, showing that legal bans don't erase cultural pressure.

punchline.text: A ritual can be sacred and violent at the same time.

quiz.question: Who led the Indian campaign against sati?
